messages.subject: reverting merges
parts:
[moved to stan-dev]


I believe that's right: once a merge has been reverted, you need to take the current develop, revert the reverted pull request, then apply changes to it. You weren't able to do that?

One reason not to rebase back to an old state is then we've lost the merges that happened after something like this happens. Hopefully we're able to catch just the last merge, but in this case, there were two merges that were applied before I caught that the build was broken.


Daniel



On Fri, May 24, 2013 at 11:21 AM, Michael Betancourt <notifi...@github.com> wrote:

@syclik Nope.

Here's the problem -- whatever revert strategy you used simply deleted the files in the reverted commit (instead of, say, rolling back to the commit before and then adding any files added in future commits) The problem is that this marks all files added in that commit as deleted. Because the head of the branch whose merge had to be committed is behind the reversion commit, those files will always be marked for deletion whenever a merge into/from develop is attempted. The reversion acts like a black hole destroying those files no matter what.

Only solution I could find was to create a new branch and recreate all of the changes from scratch. Not something we want to do every time there's a reversion -- which I hope motivates a review of the previous reversion strategy.

—

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] reverting merges
parts: I believe that's right: once a merge has been reverted, you need to take the current develop, revert the reverted pull request, then apply changes to it. You weren't able to do that?

I wasn't merging into develop, nor starting with a new branch from develop's head.  The problem is that to update the pull request I wanted to merge develop into feature/mcmc_writer -- I could merge and then unrevert but that would just restore the old mcmc_writer files because any updates are lost in the merge.

One reason not to rebase back to an old state is then we've lost the merges that happened after something like this happens. Hopefully we're able to catch just the last merge, but in this case, there were two merges that were applied before I caught that the build was broken.

Sure, I get that.  And if there have been lots of commits deleting the files from a single commit is easier than rolling back and reapplying all of the new commits.  But I don't see this allows you to keep using the reverted-branch as one normally would.

On Friday, May 24, 2013 12:31:15 PM UTC-4, Michael Betancourt wrote:
Can you be more explicit? How could I rebase without modifying origin/develop?

This is what I tried:

git checkout remotes/origin/feature/mcmc_writer
git rebase remotes/origin/develop remotes/origin/feature/mcmc_writer
# about 5 merge conflicts here, which can be solved by doing:
# edit file
# git add file
# git commit -m "fix merge conflict"
# git rebase --skip

I am not sure that 100% of your commits are there, but if they are there, then they should have different SHAs than on remotes/origin/feature/mcmc_writer. For example,

The "Slight tweak to bin/print to remove duplicate rows" commit has a different SHA now.

YMMV, so definitely try that in a detached head state before trying it on your local feature/mcmc_writer that you have been working on.

Ben
